label: lem:lc-coherent
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:lc-coherent}
Every locally compact coherent $T_0$-space is co-sober.

title: Theorem

label: lem:saturated-subspace
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:saturated-subspace}
Let $Y$ be a saturated subspace of a $T_0$-space $X$. Then the identity map induces a homeomorphism
\[
   P_{\!S}(Y)\cong\{K\in\mathcal Q(X):K\subseteq Y\},
\]
where the set on the right has the subspace topology inherited from $P_{\!S}(X)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $K\in\mathcal Q(Y)$, then $K$ is compact in $X$. If $x\in K$ and $x\leq_X z$, saturation of $Y$ gives $z\in Y$, and saturation of $K$ in $Y$ gives $z\in K$. Thus $K\in\mathcal Q(X)$ and $K\subseteq Y$. Conversely, if $K\in\mathcal Q(X)$ and $K\subseteq Y$, then compactness passes to the subspace $Y$, and saturation in $X$ implies saturation in $Y$. Hence $K\in\mathcal Q(Y)$.

The two spaces therefore have the same underlying set. If $V=U\cap Y$ is open in $Y$, where $U\in\mathcal O(X)$, then
\[
   \Box_YV=\Box_XU\capP_{\!S}(Y).
\]
Hence the upper Vietoris topologies agree.
head: environment

label: lem:kirr-subspace
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:kirr-subspace}
Let $Y$ be a saturated subspace of $X$, and let $G\in\operatorname{K\!\text{-}Irr}(X)$ satisfy $G\subseteq Y$. Then $G\in\operatorname{K\!\text{-}Irr}(Y)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Lemma~\ref{lem:saturated-subspace}, $G\in\mathcal Q(Y)$. If $G=G_1\cup G_2$ with $G_i\in\mathcal Q(Y)$, then each $G_i$ is compact saturated in $X$, again by Lemma~\ref{lem:saturated-subspace}. The $k$-irreducibility of $G$ in $X$ yields $G=G_1$ or $G=G_2$.
head: environment

label: lem:cosober-saturated
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cosober-saturated}
Every saturated subspace of a co-sober $T_0$-space is co-sober.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $Y$ be saturated in a co-sober space $X$, and let $G\in\operatorname{K\!\text{-}Irr}(Y)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:saturated-subspace}, $G\in\mathcal Q(X)$. If $G=G_1\cup G_2$ with $G_i\in\mathcal Q(X)$, then $G_i\subseteq G\subseteq Y$, and another application of Lemma~\ref{lem:saturated-subspace} gives $G_i\in\mathcal Q(Y)$. Hence $G$ is $k$-irreducible in $X$. There is therefore an $x\in X$ such that $G=\mathop{\uparrow}\!_{X}x$. Since $x\in G\subseteq Y$ and $Y$ is saturated, $\mathop{\uparrow}\!_{X}x\subseteq Y$, and hence $G=\mathop{\uparrow}\!_{Y}x$.
head: environment

label: lem:union-map
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:union-map}
For every $T_0$-space $X$, the map
\[
   \mu_X:P_{\!S}(P_{\!S}(X))\longrightarrowP_{\!S}(X),
   ~
   \mu_X(\mathcal A)=\bigcup_{K\in\mathcal A}K,
\]
is well defined and continuous.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal A\in\mathcal Q(P_{\!S}(X))$ and put $K=\bigcup\mathcal A$. The set $K$ is saturated. Let $\{U_i:i\in I\}$ be an open cover of $K$. For each $L\in\mathcal A$, choose a finite $F_L\subseteq I$ with
\[
   L\subseteq V_L:=\bigcup_{i\in F_L}U_i.
\]
The family $\{\Box_XV_L:L\in\mathcal A\}$ covers $\mathcal A$. Compactness of $\mathcal A$ yields $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in\mathcal A$ such that
\[
   \mathcal A\subseteq\Box_XV_{L_1}\cup\cdots\cup\Box_XV_{L_m}.
\]
It follows that $K\subseteq V_{L_1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{L_m}$, so $K$ is compact.

For $U\in\mathcal O(X)$,
\[
   \mu_X^{-1}(\Box_XU)
   =\left\{\mathcal A:\bigcup\mathcal A\subseteq U\right\}
   =\Box_{P_{\!S}(X)}(\Box_XU),
\]
which proves continuity.
head: environment

label: lem:iterate-principal
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $n=1$, the assertion is \eqref{eq:PSK-principal}, and $P_{\!S}^0(K)=K\in\mathcal Q(X)$. Suppose the assertion holds at level $n$. Recall that the principal saturation $\uparrow_Z z$ of any point $z$ in a topological space $Z$ is compact: if an open family covers $\uparrow_Z z$, one member contains $z$, and, being an upper set, already contains all of $\uparrow_Z z$. Hence $P_{\!S}^n(K)$, being the principal saturation of the point $P_{\!S}^{n-1}(K)$ in $P_{\!S}^n(X)$, is compact saturated. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:saturated-subspace} inside $P_{\!S}^n(X)$ gives
\[
\begin{split}
   P_{\!S}^{n+1}(K)
   &=\{\mathcal A\in\mathcal Q(P_{\!S}^n(X)):\mathcal A\subseteqP_{\!S}^n(K)\}\\
   &=\mathop{\uparrow}\!_{P_{\!S}^{n+1}(X)}P_{\!S}^n(K),
\end{split}
\]
where the last equality uses reverse inclusion at the next Smyth level.
head: environment

label: thm:carrier
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:carrier}
Let $n\geq1$, $A\inP_{\!S}^n(X)$ and $K\in\mathcal Q(X)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:carrier-criterion}
   A\inP_{\!S}^n(K)
   ~\Longleftrightarrow~
   c_n(A)\subseteq K.
\end{equation}
Consequently, $c_n(A)$ is the unique least member of $\mathcal Q(X)$, under inclusion, that carries $A$, in the sense that $A\inP_{\!S}^n(c_n(A))$ and
\[
   A\inP_{\!S}^n(K)\Longrightarrow c_n(A)\subseteq K.
\]
head: environment
name: Carrier criterion

title: Proof
body_md:
The case $n=1$ follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:saturated-subspace}, since $c_1(A)=A$. Suppose the assertion holds at level $n$, and let $\mathcal A\inP_{\!S}^{n+1}(X)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:iterate-principal},
\[
   \mathcal A\inP_{\!S}^{n+1}(K)
   ~\Longleftrightarrow~
   \mathcal A\subseteqP_{\!S}^n(K).
\]
By the induction hypothesis, this is equivalent to $c_n(A)\subseteq K$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$, which by \eqref{eq:carrier-union} is equivalent to $c_{n+1}(\mathcal A)\subseteq K$.

Taking $K=c_n(A)$ shows that $A\inP_{\!S}^n(c_n(A))$. If $A\inP_{\!S}^n(K)$ for another $K\in\mathcal Q(X)$, then \eqref{eq:carrier-criterion} gives $c_n(A)\subseteq K$.
head: environment

label: thm:localization
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Finite compact localization

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume first that $P_{\!S}^n(X)$ is co-sober. By Lemma~\ref{lem:iterate-principal}, $P_{\!S}^n(K)$ is a saturated subspace of $P_{\!S}^n(X)$ for every $K\in\mathcal Q(X)$. Hence $P_{\!S}^n(K)$ is co-sober by Lemma~\ref{lem:cosober-saturated}.

Conversely, assume (2), and let $G\in\operatorname{K\!\text{-}Irr}(P_{\!S}^n(X))$. As a compact saturated subset of $P_{\!S}^n(X)$, the set $G$ is a point of $P_{\!S}^{n+1}(X)$. Put
\[
   K=c_{n+1}(G).
\]
The carrier criterion gives $G\inP_{\!S}^{n+1}(K)$; equivalently, $G$ is a compact saturated subset of $P_{\!S}^n(K)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:iterate-principal}, $P_{\!S}^n(K)$ is saturated in $P_{\!S}^n(X)$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:kirr-subspace} therefore shows that $G$ remains $k$-irreducible in $P_{\!S}^n(K)$. Co-sobriety of $P_{\!S}^n(K)$ gives an $A\inP_{\!S}^n(K)$ such that
\[
   G=\mathop{\uparrow}\!_{P_{\!S}^n(K)}A.
\]
Since $P_{\!S}^n(K)$ is saturated in $P_{\!S}^n(X)$ and contains $A$, one has $\mathop{\uparrow}\!_{P_{\!S}^n(X)}A\subseteqP_{\!S}^n(K)$. Hence the principal saturation of $A$ is the same in the subspace and in the ambient space, and therefore
\[
   G=\mathop{\uparrow}\!_{P_{\!S}^n(X)}A.
\]
Thus $P_{\!S}^n(X)$ is co-sober.

label: lem:vietoris-compact
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:vietoris-compact}
If $C$ is compact Hausdorff, then its full Vietoris hyperspace $\mathcal K(C)$ is compact Hausdorff.
head: environment

label: lem:family-vietoris-closed
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:family-vietoris-closed}
Let $C$ be compact Hausdorff and $\mathcal A\in\mathcal Q(P_{\!S}(C))$. Then $\mathcal A$ is closed in the full Vietoris hyperspace $\mathcal K(C)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Saturation in the reverse-inclusion order means that $\mathcal A$ is hereditary under nonempty compact subsets. Let $F\in\mathcal K(C)\setminus\mathcal A$. For each $K\in\mathcal A$, one has $F\nsubseteq K$, for otherwise heredity would imply $F\in\mathcal A$. Choose $x_K\in F\setminus K$.

For every $y\in K$, choose disjoint open neighborhoods $O_y$ of $y$ and $N_y$ of $x_K$. Compactness of $K$ gives $y_1,\ldots,y_s\in K$ with
\[
   K\subseteq O_{y_1}\cup\cdots\cup O_{y_s}.
\]
Thus
\[
   V_K=O_{y_1}\cup\cdots\cup O_{y_s},
   ~
   W_K=N_{y_1}\cap\cdots\cap N_{y_s}
\]
are disjoint open sets satisfying $K\subseteq V_K$ and $x_K\in W_K$. The sets $\Box V_K$ cover $\mathcal A$ in the upper Vietoris topology. Compactness of $\mathcal A$ yields $K_1,\ldots,K_m\in\mathcal A$ such that
\[
   \mathcal A\subseteq\Box V_{K_1}\cup\cdots\cup\Box V_{K_m}.
\]
Then
\[
   N=\bigcap_{j=1}^m\Diamond W_{K_j}
\]
is a full Vietoris neighborhood of $F$. If $L\in\mathcal A$, then $L\subseteq V_{K_j}$ for some $j$, and therefore $L\cap W_{K_j}=\varnothing$. Thus $N\cap\mathcal A=\varnothing$, proving that $\mathcal A$ is closed.
head: environment

label: thm:compact-Hausdorff
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $D=\bigcup\mathcal A$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:union-map}, $D$ is a nonempty compact subset of $C$. Hence $D$ is compact Hausdorff. Every member of $\mathcal A$ is contained in $D$, so $\mathcal A\subseteqP_{\!S}(D)$. By \eqref{eq:PSK-principal}, $P_{\!S}(D)$ is a saturated subspace of $P_{\!S}(C)$; Lemmas~\ref{lem:saturated-subspace} and \ref{lem:kirr-subspace} show that $\mathcal A$ is a $k$-irreducible compact saturated subset of $P_{\!S}(D)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:family-vietoris-closed}, $\mathcal A$ is closed in $\mathcal K(D)$.

Suppose that $D\notin\mathcal A$. Since $\mathcal A$ is full-Vietoris closed, there is a basic neighborhood
\[
   \Box V\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^r\Diamond U_i
\]
of the point $D$ that is disjoint from $\mathcal A$, where $V,U_1,\ldots,U_r$ are open in $D$. The condition $D\in\Box V$ forces $V=D$, so the box condition is the whole hyperspace. Moreover, $r\geq1$, because $\mathcal A$ is nonempty. Thus each $U_i$ is nonempty and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:diamond-separation}
   D\in\bigcap_{i=1}^r\Diamond U_i,
   ~
   \mathcal A\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^r\Diamond U_i=\varnothing.
\end{equation}
For $1\leq i\leq r$, let
\[
   \mathcal A_i=\{K\in\mathcal A:K\cap U_i=\varnothing\}.
\]
Then $\mathcal A=\mathcal A_1\cup\cdots\cup\mathcal A_r$. After removing empty terms, each $\mathcal A_i$ is hereditary, and
\[
   \mathcal A_i
   =\mathcal A\cap\bigl(\mathcal K(D)\setminus\Diamond U_i\bigr)
\]
is full-Vietoris closed. Since $\mathcal K(D)$ is compact by Lemma~\ref{lem:vietoris-compact}, $\mathcal A_i$ is compact in the full Vietoris topology and hence in the coarser upper Vietoris topology. Heredity means precisely that it is saturated in $P_{\!S}(D)$, so $\mathcal A_i\in\mathcal Q(P_{\!S}(D))$.

A $k$-irreducible compact saturated set that is a finite union of compact saturated sets equals one of them, by induction on the number of terms. Hence $\mathcal A=\mathcal A_j$ for some $j$. Every member of $\mathcal A$ then misses $U_j$, so their union $D$ misses $U_j$, contradicting \eqref{eq:diamond-separation}. Therefore $D\in\mathcal A$.

Every member of $\mathcal A$ is contained in $D$, while heredity and $D\in\mathcal A$ imply that every nonempty compact subset of $D$ belongs to $\mathcal A$. Hence
\[
   \mathcal A
   =\{K\in\mathcal K(C):K\subseteq D\}
   =\mathop{\uparrow}\!_{P_{\!S}(C)}D.
\]
head: environment

label: cor:first-general
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:first-general}
Let $X$ be a $T_0$-space such that every compact saturated subspace of $X$ is Hausdorff. Then, for every $\mathcal A\in\operatorname{K\!\text{-}Irr}(P_{\!S}(X))$,
\[
   \mathcal A
   =\mathop{\uparrow}\!_{P_{\!S}(X)}\!\left(\bigcup\mathcal A\right).
\]
In particular, $P_{\!S}(X)$ is co-sober.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $D=\bigcup\mathcal A$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:union-map}, $D\in\mathcal Q(X)$, and $D$ is Hausdorff by hypothesis. The family $\mathcal A$ lies in the saturated subspace $P_{\!S}(D)$ and remains $k$-irreducible there by Lemma~\ref{lem:kirr-subspace}. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:compact-Hausdorff}. Since $P_{\!S}(D)$ is saturated in $P_{\!S}(X)$, the principal upward closure is the same in the subspace and in the ambient space.
head: environment

label: cor:first-k1
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:first-k1}
If $X$ is $k_1$-Hausdorff, then, for every $\mathcal A\in\operatorname{K\!\text{-}Irr}(P_{\!S}(X))$,
\[
   \mathcal A
   =\mathop{\uparrow}\!_{P_{\!S}(X)}\!\left(\bigcup\mathcal A\right).
\]
In particular, $P_{\!S}(X)$ is co-sober.
head: environment

label: rem:first-direct
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:first-direct}
The first-iterate conclusion for Hausdorff and metrizable spaces already follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:first-k1}. In particular, it is independent of the compact-localization theorem for higher iterates and of the stable-compactness result used in the next section.
head: environment

label: thm:stable-carriers
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:stable-carriers}
Let $X$ be a $T_0$-space such that every $K\in\mathcal Q(X)$ is stably compact as a subspace of $X$. Then $P_{\!S}^n(X)$ is co-sober for every finite $n\geq1$.
head: environment
name: Finite iterates over stably compact carriers

title: Proof
body_md: Fix $K\in\mathcal Q(X)$. By hypothesis, $K$ is stably compact. Lemma~\ref{lem:stable-preserved} implies inductively that $P_{\!S}^n(K)$ is stably compact for every finite $n\geq1$. Hence each $P_{\!S}^n(K)$ is locally compact, coherent and $T_0$, and is therefore co-sober by Lemma~\ref{lem:lc-coherent}. The result now follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:localization}.
head: environment

label: cor:Hausdorff-carriers
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:Hausdorff-carriers}
Let $X$ be a $T_0$-space such that every compact saturated subspace of $X$ is Hausdorff. Then $P_{\!S}^n(X)$ is co-sober for every finite $n\geq1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Every compact Hausdorff space is stably compact. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:stable-carriers}.
head: environment

label: cor:k1
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:k1}
If $X$ is $k_1$-Hausdorff, then $P_{\!S}^n(X)$ is co-sober for every finite $n\geq1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Every $K\in\mathcal Q(X)$ is a compact subspace of $X$ and hence Hausdorff. Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:Hausdorff-carriers}.
head: environment

label: cor:Hausdorff-metric
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:Hausdorff-metric}
If $X$ is Hausdorff, then $P_{\!S}^n(X)$ is co-sober for every finite $n\geq1$. In particular, $P_{\!S}(X)$ is co-sober. The same conclusion holds for every metrizable space.
head: environment

label: cor:sober-cosober
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:sober-cosober}
If $X$ is Hausdorff, then $P_{\!S}^n(X)$ is both sober and co-sober for every finite $n\geq1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Every Hausdorff space is sober. By Theorem~\ref{thm:sob-smyth}, sobriety is preserved by the Smyth power space, so $P_{\!S}^n(X)$ is sober for every finite $n\geq1$. Co-sobriety follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:Hausdorff-metric}.
head: environment

label: ex:cocountable
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:cocountable}
Let $X$ be an uncountable set with the co-countable topology. Any two nonempty open sets intersect, so $X$ is not Hausdorff. It is nevertheless $k_1$-Hausdorff \cite{ClontzWilliams}. For completeness, every compact subset is finite. Indeed, if $A\subseteq X$ is infinite, choose distinct points $a_1,a_2,\ldots$ in $A$ and put
\[
   U_n=X\setminus\{a_m:m\geq n\}.
\]
The sets $U_n$ form an open cover of $A$ with no finite subcover. Thus every compact subspace is finite and hence Hausdorff.

The space $X$ is not sober: $X$ itself is an irreducible closed set, but, since the topology is $T_1$, it is not the closure of a point. Hence every $P_{\!S}^n(X)$ with $n\geq1$ is co-sober by Corollary~\ref{cor:k1} and non-sober by repeated application of Theorem~\ref{thm:sob-smyth}.
head: environment
